newsitem.title: USA: California panel lauds NAFTA, urges Chile's entry.
newsitem.headline: California panel lauds NAFTA, urges Chile's entry.

text.p: A California commission on Tuesday called the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) an "unquestionable success" and urged the Clinton administration to move quickly to bring Chile into the pact.

The California World Trade Commission, which advises Republican Gov. Pete Wilson on international trade issues, said NAFTA boosted the state's exports to Mexico and Canada by billions of dollars since 1993, when the three-way trade agreement was approved.

These exports, in turn, have created tens of thousands of jobs in California, helping the most populous U.S. state recover from a recent recession and weather deep cuts in federal spending on aerospace and defense contracts.
"In terms of trade, NAFTA has been an unquestionable success for both the United States and California," the commission said in its report.

To expand on these gains, the commission called for the United States to extend fast-track negotiating authority so Chile could become the next NAFTA member. Fast-track authority allows U.S. officials to negotiate trade deals without fear that Congress will change them. Lawmakers would be able to vote for an agreement or against it, but could not amend it.
By admitting Chile, the U.S. would boost trade and send a signal to the rest of Latin America that free-market policies will be rewarded, the commission said.

"That means clear authority -- no dithering and delaying, no conditions regarding labor and environmental standards. Fast-track authority, plain and simple," said Wilson, one of the few Republicans who supported NAFTA from its inception.
The commission's report, based on a three-year review of NAFTA's impact on California, was presented Tuesday to members of Congress and the Mexican Ambassador to the United States.
Under NAFTA, California exports to Mexico have grown $2.6 billion, reaching $9.1 billion in 1996, according to the commission's 51-page report.
Today, California exports to Mexico support 126,000 jobs in the state, with 23,800 of these jobs resulting from export growth in 1996 alone, the report said.
Since the 1988 U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement, which preceded NAFTA, California exports to Canada have increased 177 percent, or $7.1 billion, to exceed $11 billion in 1996.

The commission concluded that $3.4 billion of this export growth came during the three years since NAFTA's implementation. Export growth to Canada under NAFTA has supported 47,000 California jobs, the report said.

"We now see a variety of industries flourishing -- electronics, tourism, agriculture, power generation, consumer goods and textiles -- significantly because of new markets created by the free-trade pact," Wilson said.
"The time has come to end the stalling and approve authority for fast-track negotiations with Chile, to facilitate that nation's accession to NAFTA," the governor said.
